brazil.intro:
Brazil is a huge country of beaches, rainforest, big cities and strong regional food traditions. Eating out is social, relaxed and often built around grilled meat, fresh fruit and rich stews.

This page explains what Brazil is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Brazil is known for Rio's beaches and Christ the Redeemer, the Amazon rainforest, Iguazu Falls, football, samba and Carnival. Each region has its own culture, from the African influenced northeast to the German and Italian influenced south.

The country has a warm, friendly dining culture, with long lunches and lively evenings.

Feijoada, a black bean and pork stew served with rice, collard greens and orange, is the national dish. Churrasco, grilled meat served at the table, is a southern tradition, and pao de queijo, cheese bread, is a snack everywhere. Moqueca, a coconut fish stew, is a northeast favorite.

Sweet treats include brigadeiros, chocolate truffles, and acai bowls. Caipirinha, made with cachaca and lime, is the national cocktail, and fresh juices are sold on every corner.

Rio de Janeiro offers beaches, mountains and samba, Salvador has colonial streets and Afro Brazilian culture, and Sao Paulo is the great food city. Iguazu Falls, the Amazon near Manaus, Florianopolis beaches and the colonial towns of Minas Gerais are other highlights.

Brasilia is famous for its modern architecture.

Amazonas is the largest Brazilian state, covering a huge part of the Amazon rainforest. Its food is shaped by the river and the forest.

sections.body:
The state is known for the Amazon river, the meeting of waters near Manaus, where two rivers of different colors flow side by side, and for rainforest lodges and jungle tours. Indigenous traditions remain strong in food and craft.

The climate is hot and humid all year.

River fish such as tambaqui, pirarucu and tucunare are grilled, fried or cooked in stews. Tacaca, a hot soup with shrimp and tapioca gum, and tucupi, a yellow sauce from cassava, are local specialties. Fruits such as acai, cupuacu and guarana are used in juices and desserts.

Cassava flour, called farinha, accompanies many meals.

Manaus has the Teatro Amazonas opera house and the Meeting of the Waters. Jungle lodges and river cruises offer wildlife, and Anavilhanas archipelago has quiet river islands. The Presidente Figueiredo area has waterfalls.

The Amazon fish market is a lively sight.

sections.body:
The city is known for the Teatro Amazonas, a grand opera house built in the rubber boom, the Adolpho Lisboa market and the Meeting of the Waters, where the dark Rio Negro joins the sandy Solimoes. It sits in the middle of the jungle.

It is hot and humid, and rain falls often.

Try tambaqui ribs, grilled pirarucu and tucunare, along with tacaca soup, tucupi and jambu, a leaf that makes the mouth tingle. Breakfast often includes tapioca crepes and regional fruit juices. Acai here is eaten savory with fish and farinha.

Cupuacu and guarana sweets are good gifts.

The Teatro Amazonas, the Adolpho Lisboa market, the Meeting of the Waters and the Rio Negro Palace are the main sights. Day trips and jungle lodges are arranged from the city. Presidente Figueiredo has waterfalls.

The Ponta Negra beach is popular at sunset.

Bahia is the soul of Afro Brazilian culture, with colonial towns, music, long beaches and some of the most distinctive food in the country.

sections.body:
The state is known for Salvador, with its colorful old town, for Carnival and for traditions such as capoeira and candomble. The long coast has beaches from Porto Seguro to the Chapada Diamantina hills inland.

The food shows African, Indigenous and Portuguese roots.

Moqueca baiana, a fish stew with coconut milk, palm oil and peppers, is a signature dish. Acaraje, fried bean fritters stuffed with shrimp and spicy paste, is sold on the street by women in white dress. Vatapa, caruru and bobo de camarao are other rich dishes.

Coconut sweets and fresh fruit complete the meal.

Salvador's Pelourinho, the Lacerda Elevator and the beaches are classic. Porto Seguro has the Arraial d'Ajuda area, and Morro de Sao Paulo and Praia do Forte have beaches. The Chapada Diamantina offers waterfalls and caves.

Carnival and Sao Joao festivals are big events.

sections.h2: What Porto Seguro is known for
sections.body:
The town is known for its historic upper town, with colorful houses and a view of the sea, and for beaches such as Taperapua. Nearby are the villages of Arraial d'Ajuda and Trancoso, which have a hippie chic style.

The area has lively evenings and beach parties.

Beach huts called barracas serve grilled fish, shrimp, moqueca and cold coconut water. Local dishes use coconut milk, palm oil and fresh seafood. Tapioca pancakes, acai and fruit juices are common at breakfast.

Trancoso has a charming square with restaurants.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Porto Seguro
sections.body:
The Cidade Historica, the Praia de Taperapua and the Arraial d'Ajuda village are the highlights. Trancoso and Caraiva are quieter beach villages, and Monte Pascoal National Park has hills and forests.

Boat trips go to coral reefs and beaches.

Salvador is the capital of Bahia and the first capital of Brazil. It is the heart of Afro Brazilian culture, with food, music and religion on every street.

This page explains what Salvador is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for Pelourinho, a World Heritage old town with colorful colonial buildings, for the Lacerda Elevator and for its Carnival, one of the largest in the world. Drum groups, capoeira and street music fill the evenings.

The bay and the beaches add a seaside feel.

Acaraje, fried bean fritters filled with shrimp and vatapa, is the classic street food. Moqueca baiana, vatapa, caruru and bobo de camarao are rich with coconut milk and palm oil. Fresh fish and shellfish are widely available.

Sweets include cocada, coconut candy, and quindim, a baked custard.

Pelourinho, the Church of Sao Francisco, the Lacerda Elevator and the Farol da Barra lighthouse are the highlights. The Mercado Modelo is good for crafts, and the Bonfim Church is a pilgrimage site. Beaches such as Porto da Barra are popular for sunsets.

Ilha de Itaparica is a ferry ride away.

Pelourinho has many restaurants, with live music in the evening.

Take care at night and use registered taxis or apps. Hills and cobblestones make walking tiring, so wear comfortable shoes. Ask about spice levels.

Ceara is a northeastern state with a long sunny coast, wind swept dunes and fishing villages. It is known for kitesurfing and relaxed beach life.

sections.body:
The state is known for Fortaleza, its lively capital, and for beaches such as Jericoacoara, Canoa Quebrada and Praia do Futuro. The wind is strong and steady, which makes the coast a world class kitesurfing spot.

Ceara has a lively music scene and forro dances.

Seafood is central, with lobster, shrimp, crab and grilled fish. Carne de sol, sun dried beef, tapioca, cassava dishes and baiao de dois, rice with beans, are traditional. Fresh coconut water, cashew juice and rapadura, a sugar cane sweet, are common.

Beach huts serve grilled fish with farofa.

Fortaleza has beaches and a night market, Jericoacoara has dunes and sunset climbs, and Canoa Quebrada has red cliffs. Cumbuco and Prea are known for wind sports. Lencois Maranhenses is a long drive east.

The interior has hills and cooler weather.

sections.body:
The city is known for Praia do Futuro and Iracema, for its night craft market, forro music and a sunny climate all year. The seafront is lively, with restaurants, bars and street vendors.

People here are friendly and love to talk and dance.

Seafood is the star, with lobster, crab, shrimp and grilled fish. Beach shacks at Praia do Futuro serve fish with farofa, and carne de sol, tapioca and cassava dishes are local classics. Cashew juice, coconut water and rapadura sweets are common.

Crab stew and fried fish are favorite beach meals.

Iracema Beach and the Ponte dos Ingleses, the Dragao do Mar cultural center, the Mucuripe fish market and the Praia do Futuro are popular. Beach Park, a water park, is close.

Cumbuco and Canoa Quebrada are day trips.

Jericoacoara is a small beach village between dunes and the sea, famous for its sunsets, its wind and its relaxed pace. Streets are sand, and cars are not allowed in the village center.

sections.body:
The village is known for the Sunset Dune, where people gather each evening, for the Pedra Furada rock arch and for kitesurfing. It is part of a national park, and it feels remote and informal.

In the evening, the main street fills with live music, tapas and cocktails.

Fresh seafood and grilled fish are the basics, along with lobster, shrimp, tapioca and fruit juices. Many restaurants serve pizza, pasta and international dishes for visitors. Caipirinhas and coconut water are everywhere.

Beach bars serve snacks at sunset.

The Sunset Dune, Pedra Furada, the Tatajuba village and the Lagoa Azul and Lagoa Paraiso lagoons are the highlights. Buggy tours cover the dunes and lagoons, and kitesurfing and windsurfing lessons are common.

Horse rides and sunset walks are also popular.

sections.h2: What Federal District is known for
sections.body:
The district is known for Oscar Niemeyer's modern architecture, wide avenues and the monumental axis of government buildings. The planned city is divided into sectors, and each has its own shopping and dining areas.

The region is also home to parks, lakes and ecological reserves.

Look for central Brazilian dishes such as pequi rice, a fruit with a strong flavor, galinhada, chicken and rice, and pamonha, a corn paste. Churrasco steak houses are very popular, and bakeries sell pao de queijo and coffee. Government workers and diplomats bring international tastes.

Lake side restaurants serve fish and casual food.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Federal District
sections.body:
The Cathedral, the National Congress, the Palace of the Dawn and the Juscelino Kubitschek Memorial are highlights. Lake Paranoa is a leisure area with sunset spots, and the Dom Bosco Sanctuary glows in blue light.

National Park of Brasilia has pools and trails.

Distances are long, so use ride apps. The dry season from May to September is very dry, so drink water. Tip about 10 percent where service is not added.

The state is known for its colonial towns built during the gold rush, such as Ouro Preto and Tiradentes, and for its coffee, cheese and cachaca. Belo Horizonte is the capital and a lively city of bars and music.

Farm kitchens and wood stoves are part of the local identity.

Mineiro cuisine is hearty, with pao de queijo, feijao tropeiro, beans with sausage and eggs, tutu de feijao, frango com quiabo, chicken with okra, and pork dishes. Minas cheese, especially Canastra, is famous, and doce de leite and fruit preserves are everywhere.

The Botanical Garden, the Museu Oscar Niemeyer, the Ópera de Arame and the Rua XV are highlights. Santa Felicidade is good for a family lunch, and the Serra Verde train to Morretes is a scenic day trip.

Street food includes acaraje and fried snacks.

Recife has the old center, the Instituto Ricardo Brennand and beaches. Olinda is a hilltop colonial city, and Porto de Galinhas has reefs and pools. Fernando de Noronha is a protected island.

sections.h2: What Rio de Janeiro is known for
sections.body:
The city is known for Copacabana and Ipanema beaches, Sugarloaf Mountain, Christ the Redeemer, samba and Carnival. Neighborhoods such as Lapa, Santa Teresa and Leblon each have a distinct character.

Life happens outdoors, from beach volleyball to open air bars.

Feijoada on Saturdays is a ritual, usually with caipirinha. Botecos serve cold beer with fried snacks, such as pasteis, bolinhos de bacalhau and coxinhas. Fresh seafood, grilled fish, acai bowls, coconut water and juices are everywhere.

Churrascarias and por quilo places are good for lunch.

sections.h2: What Santa Catarina is known for
sections.body:
The state is known for Florianopolis, on an island with dozens of beaches, and for Blumenau, with its Oktoberfest. The coast has surf beaches and fishing villages, and the hills have wine and cool weather.

The pace is relaxed and outdoorsy.

Oysters are farmed on the island and eaten fresh, along with shrimp and fish. Tainha, mullet, is a seasonal specialty, and the German towns serve sausages, cakes and beer. Pirao, a fish porridge, and fresh seafood stews are local.

Wine from the highland vineyards is a growing treat.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Santa Catarina
sections.body:
Florianopolis offers beaches such as Joaquina and Campeche, the lagoon and old fishing villages. Blumenau has German architecture, Balneario Camboriu has high rises and beaches, and Gramado is just north in Rio Grande do Sul.

The Serra Catarinense has snow in winter.

Florianopolis is a city on an island, with over forty beaches, lagoons and fishing villages. It is loved for its surfing, nature and seafood.

The city is known for beaches such as Joaquina, Campeche and Jurere, for the Lagoa da Conceicao and the Azorean heritage of its old villages. The island has wide dunes, hiking trails and a lively summer.

Oysters and seafood are everywhere.

Fresh oysters from Ribeirao da Ilha are the highlight, along with shrimp, fish and pirao. Tainha, mullet, is a winter specialty, and seafood buffets are common. Cafes serve coffee, tapioca and cakes, and craft beer is growing.

Waterfront restaurants offer sunset views.

Joaquina Beach, the Lagoa da Conceicao, the Santo Antonio de Lisboa village and Ribeirao da Ilha are popular. Hiking trails lead to hidden beaches, and the Hercilio Luz Bridge is a landmark.

In winter, whale watching is possible nearby.

Sao Paulo state is the economic center of Brazil, with a giant capital city, coastal beaches and hill towns.

sections.h2: What São Paulo is known for
sections.body:
The state is known for Sao Paulo, the largest city in the country, and for beaches such as Ubatuba and Ilhabela. Santos and Campos do Jordao add port and mountain experiences.

Immigrants from Italy, Japan, Lebanon and Portugal have shaped the food scene.

Sao Paulo is known for pizza, mortadella sandwiches, pastel and Japanese food. Lebanese kibbeh, Italian pasta and Portuguese bacalhau are common, and feijoada and churrasco are classics. On the coast, fresh seafood and fish stews are popular.

Coffee has deep roots in the state.

sections.h2: Places to visit in São Paulo
sections.body:
The city has Avenida Paulista, the Ibirapuera Park and museums. Santos has a coffee museum and port, Ilhabela and Ubatuba have beaches and forests, and Campos do Jordao has cool mountain air and fondue.

Coffee farms around the interior welcome visitors.

People here love eating out, from street stalls to fine dining.

Street food includes pastel, coxinha and tapioca.
